entry.evidence: Thus, it is especially important to monitor PSCs on a long-term basis.

sequences.source_document: Published paper (XML text, PDF for figures)

steps.action: The authors pose the need for long-term, ground-based monitoring of PSC occurrence as a complement to satellites and cloud-affected lidars.
steps.quote: Thus, it is especially important to monitor PSCs on a long-term basis.

steps.action: The authors use existing zenith DOAS instruments at Neumayer (since 1999) and Kiruna (since 1996), built and described in the group's earlier work for trace-gas retrievals.
steps.quote: It has been almost continuously operating since 1999

steps.action: The authors check the instrument records for degradation using the spectra and summer-month interannual variation, and correct for offset and dark current.
steps.quote: there is no indication of instrument degradation for either instrument, as seen from an examination of the spectra

steps.action: The authors adapt the colour-index method (after Sarkissian et al. 1991), choosing 390/340 nm and 610/444 nm ratios averaged over 93.0-94.5 degrees SZA and correlated with ECMWF 50 hPa temperature.
steps.quote: the CI is calculated for the ratios of intensities at 390 to 340 nm in the UV

steps.action: The authors test the earlier processing choice of normalising the CI at SZA = 90 degrees and confirm that it is not beneficial, as found by Enell et al. (2002).
steps.quote: The same finding could be confirmed in the current study.

steps.action: The authors use McArtim Monte Carlo radiative transfer runs for a horizontally homogeneous PSC layer to compute the expected CI against SZA for several optical depths and altitudes, with and without a tropospheric cloud (UV reduction, visible maximum, cloud enhancement).
steps.quote: the CI is reduced in the UV (upper panel) in the presence of a PSC

steps.action: Prompted by Gomez-Martin and Toledo, the authors run 3D simulations of confined and hemispheric PSCs of different extents and show that localised PSCs reverse the UV signal while extents of 10 degrees or more match the homogeneous case.
steps.quote: The horizontal extent of the PSC is impacting the simulations, as pointed out by Laura Gomez-Martin and Daniel Toledo (personal communication, 2021).

steps.action: The authors vary the Angstrom exponent, the phase function (Henyey-Greenstein g values and a Mie phase function), the atmospheric profiles and the albedo, and find small effects.
steps.quote: However, the effect of changing the parameter settings remains small for both spectral ranges.

steps.action: The authors define a PSC detection threshold from the summer-month CI minimum (UV) or maximum (visible), averaged over instrument periods, with the standard deviation as error.
steps.quote: a CI threshold can be defined for the detection of PSCs from the measured spectra

steps.action: The authors compare the mean measured CI of PSC, non-PSC and baseline cases at Neumayer with the 1D simulations and find good agreement, consistent with PSC optical depths of 0.005-0.01 at 20-22 km.
steps.quote: It shows a good overall agreement.

steps.action: The authors repeat the simulation-measurement comparison for the Arctic station Kiruna and find similar agreement.
steps.quote: A similarly good agreement is also found for the Kiruna station

steps.action: The authors plot CI against ECMWF 50 hPa temperature for single years at both stations and observe a distinct seasonal cycle, including signals in late spring.
steps.quote: A distinctive seasonal cycle is seen for either station.

steps.action: For the presumed PSC cases in spring at Kiruna, when temperatures are high, the authors propose volcanically induced aerosol as an alternative source of the signal.
steps.quote: namely the influence by volcanically induced aerosol particles

steps.action: The authors compare the UV and visible retrievals and the cloud-filtered and unfiltered Neumayer data, and find that cloud filtering lowers the detected PSC count but leaves the seasonal cycle unchanged.
steps.quote: Nonetheless, the course of the seasonal cycle is not affected by tropospheric cloud contamination.

steps.action: The authors compare monthly PSC relative frequencies with CALIOP and MIPAS climatologies sampled near the stations, and find agreement except for higher DOAS occurrence in spring.
steps.quote: In general, the data (especially in the UV) agree well with the satellite retrievals.

steps.action: The authors derive biweekly and yearly PSC relative frequencies at Neumayer for 1999-2021 (about 37 percent UV, 21 percent visible) with asymmetric errors, and test for a trend.
steps.quote: There is no significant trend throughout the measurement period.

steps.action: The authors compare the time series with the known stratospheric sudden warmings of 2002 and 2019, both of which show reduced PSC sightings.
steps.quote: The rapid increase in temperature and thus reduced PSC sightings are also reported by the DOAS data

steps.action: The authors rerun the Neumayer analysis with the O4-based tropospheric cloud filter to estimate the cloud-induced error (about 20 percent higher frequency in the UV).
steps.quote: the retrieved PSC relative frequency is about 20 % higher in the UV when applying the filter

steps.action: The authors derive the Kiruna PSC relative frequency time series (about 18 percent on average) and find no trend.
steps.quote: On average, a PSC relative frequency of about 18 % is detected above Kiruna.

steps.action: The authors note recurrent high PSC-like springtime signatures at Kiruna (2014/15, 2018/19, 2019/20) together with reduced total ozone in ECMWF and MERRA2.
steps.quote: High PSC-like signatures are also found towards springtime

steps.action: The authors use the ALOMAR lidar background-aerosol seasonal cycle (Langenbach et al. 2019) to exclude natural background-aerosol variation, because its August-October maximum is absent from the DOAS signal.
steps.quote: Natural seasonal variation of the stratospheric background aerosol can thus be excluded as a possible explanation of the springtime signature.

steps.action: The authors identify natural test cases in the OMPS-LP extinction record: the Kelut/Sangeang Api (2014), Ambae (2018), Raikoke (2019) and Calbuco (2015) eruptions.
steps.quote: Three eruptions in particular are likely observed by the DOAS instrument.

steps.action: The authors match each tropical or northern eruption with a springtime PSC-like signal the following year at Kiruna, and the southern Calbuco eruption with the Neumayer 2015 enhancement only.
steps.quote: a high PSC-like signature is found during springtime the following year

steps.action: As contrasts, the authors check the wildfire smoke events, which leave no DOAS signature, and inspect the vortex position, whose passages over Kiruna coincide with the enhanced signals.
steps.quote: exhibit no signatures in the DOAS measurements due to the different particle size distribution

steps.action: The authors keep the CI method as a characterized tool for consistent long-term PSC occurrence statistics, with known underestimation from tropospheric clouds and lower sensitivity in the visible.
steps.quote: the presented approach allows for a consistent investigation of PSC occurrences above the measurement stations

steps.action: The authors keep volcanic aerosol as the explanation of the unexpected springtime signatures.
steps.quote: could be explained by induced volcanic aerosol particles in the stratosphere after large eruptions

end.claim: The zenith-sky colour-index method, characterized with McArtim simulations and satellite comparisons, yields consistent multi-decadal PSC occurrence statistics (about 37 percent at Neumayer and 18 percent at Kiruna, no trend), with known underestimation from tropospheric clouds and lower sensitivity in the visible.

decisive_move.sentence: The McArtim simulations of the CI response to PSCs (a UV decrease and a visible maximum at SZA above 90 degrees for extended layers) provide the basis for the sign and the threshold of the detection, without which the measured CI could not be read as PSC occurrence.

gates.evidence: The DOAS data were collected over 20+ years for trace-gas retrievals, so no hypothesis directed their acquisition (§2 ¶1). The method faced comparisons it could have failed: simulations (§3.2 ¶2), CALIOP and MIPAS (§4.1 ¶3), and the 2002/2019 sudden warmings (§5 ¶3). The volcanic explanation faced the exclusion of background aerosol (§6 ¶4) but no decisive test. Thresholds were set from summer data during the analysis, and nothing was fixed in advance (§3.2 ¶1).

Mercury lamp spectrum for wavelength calibration

but is not captured by other PSC climatologies
which is a decisive advance compared to measurements with limited temporal coverage, e.g. satellite observations

limits: No review file was supplied, although the paper was reviewed (by Sarkissian and one anonymous referee), so no review sequence is coded and any referee-forced changes are invisible. The paper does not report how the wavelength pairs were chosen against the earlier pairs beyond avoiding Fraunhofer lines and ozone absorption. The 3D-extent simulations were prompted by a personal communication, coded as trigger commenter. Sub-claims at other statuses: the PSC relative frequencies and the absence of a trend are estimate_with_resolution (Tables 1-2, §5 ¶2, §6 ¶2); the volcanic aerosol explanation of the springtime signals is best_explanation, based on visual coincidence with three eruptions and no statistical test (§6.1 ¶2, §7 ¶4). The trend test method is not stated. The authors themselves doubt the late-spring Neumayer PSCs because of sedimentation (§4 ¶2), so the spring frequencies may include non-PSC particles. Composition is coded capability_first by inference: the method and record are not new, but the walk goes characterization, then application, then the emergent springtime question and its rivals. A trace_series reading would fit the volcanic sub-walk.

disagreements.target: Sarkissian et al. (1991) and Enell et al. (1999): normalising the CI to its value at SZA = 90 degrees
disagreements.support: The authors re-examine the normalisation in their own data and, like Enell et al. (2002), find that it does not help.
disagreements.quote: However, in a later study this was found not to be beneficial.

disagreements.target: Gomez-Martin et al. (2021): PSC altitude from the position of the CI maximum
disagreements.support: 3D simulations show that the altitude signal holds only for confined PSCs and fades for horizontally extended layers; it also requires high temporal resolution.
disagreements.quote: However, high temporal resolution of the measurements and special PSC conditions are needed to be able to infer the CI maximum with sufficient accuracy

disagreements.support: DOAS shows higher springtime occurrence than the satellite climatologies, which the authors attribute to volcanic aerosol, supported by OMPS-LP extinction.
disagreements.quote: but is not captured by other PSC climatologies

disagreements.target: Stratospheric aerosol climatologies from satellite data
disagreements.support: Springtime particles detected by DOAS after eruptions are argued to be missing from existing climatologies.
disagreements.quote: is not yet fully captured by the stratospheric aerosol climatologies from satellite data

alternatives_considered.alternatives: 550/350 nm (Sarkissian et al. 1991); 680/385 nm (Enell et al. 1999, 2002)
alternatives_considered.reason: Avoid strong Fraunhofer lines and ozone absorption; only wavelengths larger than 330 nm

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Normalising the CI to its value at SZA = 90 degrees
alternatives_considered.reason: Found not to be beneficial (Enell et al. 2002), confirmed here

alternatives_considered.chosen: CI averaged between 93.0 and 94.5 degrees SZA
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Position of the CI maximum (Gomez-Martin et al. 2021)
alternatives_considered.reason: Locating the maximum needs high temporal resolution and special PSC conditions

alternatives_considered.chosen: 1D horizontally homogeneous PSC layer as the standard configuration
alternatives_considered.alternatives: 3D confined 2x2 degree PSC, 2 degree belt, and 1, 5 and 10 degree hemispheric PSCs
alternatives_considered.reason: Large horizontal extent of typical (non-lee-wave) PSCs; Antarctic PSC area extends to about 65 degrees S

alternatives_considered.chosen: Henyey-Greenstein phase function with g = 0.7, Angstrom exponent 2
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Other g values, a Mie phase function, alpha = 0, other atmospheric profiles and albedo
alternatives_considered.reason: g = 0.7 corresponds to particle sizes of 0.3 to 10 micrometres
These data sets were readily available

alternatives_considered.chosen: CI threshold averaged over the whole series per instrument period
alternatives_considered.reason: Allows equal treatment of all years in the time series

alternatives_considered.chosen: Modified O4-DSCD cloud filter with a 75th-percentile threshold
alternatives_considered.alternatives: MAX-DOAS cloud classification scheme of Wagner et al. (2014, 2016)
alternatives_considered.reason: Existing scheme is affected by high surface albedo and optimised for SZA below 80 degrees

alternatives_considered.chosen: Unfiltered Neumayer analysis as main result, filtered analysis for error estimate
alternatives_considered.reason: Cloud filtering leads to underestimation of PSC cases

alternatives_considered.alternatives: O4-based filter or an alternative filter
alternatives_considered.reason: No clear correlation between O4 DSCDs and ECMWF cloud fraction; clouds less critical for the UV threshold

alternatives_considered.chosen: CALIOP only for the Kiruna comparison
alternatives_considered.reason: No temporal overlap between CALIOP, MIPAS and the DOAS data
